original_value: The buffer generation algorithm is a fundamental function in GIS, identifying areas of a given distance surrounding geographic features. Past research largely focused on buffer generation algorithms generated in a stand-alone environment. Moreover, dissolved buffer generation is data- and computing-intensive. In this scenario, the improvement in the stand-alone environment is limited when considering large-scale mass vector data. Nevertheless, recent parallel dissolved vector buffer algorithms suffer from scalability problems, leaving room for further optimization. At present, the prevailing in-memory cluster-computing framework—Spark—provides promising efficiency for computing-intensive analysis; however, it has seldom been researched for buffer analysis. On this basis, we propose a cluster-computing-oriented parallel dissolved vector buffer generating algorithm, called the HPBM, that contains a Hilbert-space-filling-curve-based data partition method, a data skew and cross-boundary objects processing strategy, and a depth-given tree-like merging method. Experiments are conducted in both stand-alone and cluster environments using real-world vector data that include points and roads. Compared with some existing parallel buffer algorithms, as well as various popular GIS software, the HPBM achieves a performance gain of more than 50%.

result.paraphrase: Buffer generation is a core GIS operation for identifying areas at a specified distance around geographic features. Prior studies have mostly examined buffer-generation methods in stand-alone settings. In addition, dissolved buffer generation is both data-intensive and compute-intensive, so improvements in a stand-alone environment are limited for large-scale vector data. Meanwhile, existing parallel dissolved vector buffer algorithms have scalability issues, leaving room for optimization. Today, the widely used in-memory cluster-computing framework Spark offers promising efficiency for compute-intensive analysis, but it has rarely been studied for buffer analysis. Based on this, we present HPBM, a parallel dissolved vector buffer generation algorithm oriented to cluster computing. It includes a Hilbert-space-filling-curve-based data partitioning method, a strategy for handling data skew and cross-boundary objects, and a depth-specified tree-like merging method. Experiments were carried out in both stand-alone and cluster environments with real-world vector data, including points and roads. Compared with several existing parallel buffer algorithms and various popular GIS software packages, HPBM delivers a performance improvement of over 50%.
